name: Yemenite

database_scope.purpose: Sourced reference for Yemenite minhagim and halachic practice. It records what the cited sources say, with a confidence level for each entry, and is not a psak.
database_scope.coverage_note: 38 sourced topics and 7 distinctive customs, compiled from the cited sources in October 2026. Each entry carries a confidence level (well-attested, disputed, regional, needs-review). 12 topics have no community-specific source and are listed under 'gaps' rather than filled with generic text.

identity.primary_origin: Yemen, with Sana'a as its leading community

languages: Aramaic: the Omer count is said in Aramaic
Arabic: a child may ask the Mah Nishtanah in Arabic, and women recite an afternoon Arabic lamentation
Hebrew, Arabic and Aramaic: the paraliturgical anthology sung at Shabbat meals and celebrations

subgroups.name: Baladi (בלדי)
subgroups.note: ‘Local’ rite as copied in Yemen in manuscript Tiklalim; Mishneh Torah is the leading authority. Most Baladi worshippers follow the text fixed by Maharitz (R. Yihya Salah) in Etz Hayyim. Geridi: an unqualified ‘Yemenite siddur’ means the Baladi one.

subgroups.name: Shami (שאמי)
subgroups.note: ‘Eretz-Israel’ rite, essentially the Sephardic siddur with some Baladi retentions; also accepts Shulchan Aruch. Sar-Shalom: where Shami do not follow Baladi they generally follow Sephardic custom. Shami still follow the Tiklal for Seder additions, Shavuot, Hoshanot and selichot (Geridi).

subgroups.name: Dor Daim (דרדעים / Dor De'ah)
subgroups.note: Rambam-centered movement of R. Yihya Qafih, continued in scholarship by R. Yosef Qafih; Sar-Shalom: they preserve elements of Saadia Gaon's siddur with the Rambam's rulings. No longer an organized movement. Distinct documented practices are few in the sources opened.

timeline.event: Yemenite siddurim had no Kabbalat Shabbat; the Shabbat evening service began with Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbat.
timeline.halachic_impact: Lekha Dodi and Kabbalat Shabbat entered from printed books from the early 17th century (Gavra).

timeline.event: Shami (Sephardic-printed) influence spread under R. Shalom ben Aharon ha-Kohen Iraqi ‘al-Usta’ (1685–1780), Nasi of the Sana'a community, who according to the Encyclopedia of Yemenite Sages (teman.org.il) urged the switch from the Yemenite to the Sephardic siddur around 1728 (תפ״ח), causing a major dispute; Mori Yehuda Tza'di and Mori Pinchas ben Shlomo Iraqi opposed him, and his synagogue Knis al-Usta became the Shami centre. Maharitz wrote Etz Hayyim to anchor Baladi custom.
timeline.halachic_impact: Parallel Baladi and Shami rites in the same towns.

timeline.event: First printing of the Baladi Tiklal in Jerusalem with Etz Hayyim.
Dor De'ah circle around R. Yihya Qafih.
timeline.halachic_impact: Rambam-only, anti-Kabbalistic tendency; later partly reabsorbed into Baladi.

timeline.event: R. Yosef Qafih publishes Tiklalim Shivat Tzion (5712) and Siach Yerushalayim (5755), whose notes mark Baladi/Shami differences.

Many Yemenite customs lapsed or were replaced; e.g., Geridi (Pesach §1): in Israel the special Pesach preparations made in Yemen lapsed, and only in some villages do Yemenites still bake matzah at home daily.
timeline.halachic_impact: Gap between ancient custom and current Israeli Yemenite practice.

primary_codes: Rambam, Mishneh Torah (Yemenite manuscript text, R. Yosef Qafih edition)
later_poskim: R. Yosef Qafih (Shivat Tzion, Siach Yerushalayim; Halikhot Teiman)
core_halachic_authorities.decision_principle: Baladi and Dor Daim: Rambam as binding decisor, but inherited Yemenite custom is preserved even where it diverges; Shami: Shulchan Aruch and Sephardic custom where not following Baladi. Zohar Amar (Sefer HaChilukim) stresses there is no single uniform Baladi custom.

runtime.practice_baseline: Baladi and Dor Daim practice rests on the Rambam's Mishneh Torah and the Tiklal (Maharitz / Qafih editions); Shami practice adds the Shulchan Aruch and Sephardic siddur.
